extracted.intended_audience: learned readers, artists, natural philosophers, and speakers (Renaissance-era/early modern audience)
extracted.subtask_short: philosophical aphorisms on nature and art
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of numbered aphorisms and short discourses about nature, knowledge, the senses, experience, art, and speaking—offering evaluative maxims and practical counsel for learners, creators, and speakers. Not a formal how-to but a set of principles one might apply to learning, observing, and creating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience as primary guide
rubrics_metrics.description: In my subjects experience is a truer guide than the words of others; experience was the teacher of all great writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly argued (24,25,31): rely on one's own experience for judgement and creative work rather than merely quoting authorities; cite 'experience' as the superior source. Example/contrast: humanists who parade others' labours vs creators who draw on experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute authority for intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: He who in reasoning cites authority is making use of his memory rather than of his intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for reasoning founded on observation and intellect rather than mere appeals to authority (26). Anti-pattern: relying on named authorities instead of testing claims by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value creators over commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who are creators and interpreters of nature ... must be judged and esteemed like the object before the mirror as compared with its image reflected in the mirror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators (originators, inventors) are intrinsically more valuable than boastful exploiters of others' works (27,29). For evaluation: prioritize originality and making over mere commentary or compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ancient models to modern fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to imitate ancient than modern work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct injunction to look to ancient exemplars when imitating or learning (30). Implies evaluating works against lasting classical standards rather than recent trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom arises from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom is the daughter of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short maxim (31) reinforcing that practical acquaintance with phenomena yields true understanding; use empirical grounding when judging ideas or art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience does not err; judgements do
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience never errs; it is only your judgements that err, ye who look to her for effects which our experiments cannot produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between correct empirical observation and mistaken inference (32–33). When a predicted effect fails, consider impediments or faulty interpretation rather than blaming observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid precepts not confirmed by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the precepts of those thinkers whose reasoning is not confirmed by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discard or distrust doctrines that lack experiential verification (40). For creative or scholarly work, favour empirically grounded methods and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer small useful truths to grand falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: Man discourseth greatly, and his discourse is for the greater part empty and false; the discourse of animals is small, but useful and true: slender certainty is better than portentous falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating speech, prose, or theory, favour concise, useful truth over elaborate but false or empty rhetoric (41). Anti-pattern: valuing pompous style over substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abridge studies; completeness over premature brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who seek to abbreviate studies do injury to knowledge and to love ... impatience, the mother of stupidity, praises brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues (48) against superficial abridgement of complex subjects; advocates thorough study of parts to form complete understanding. Example: criticizing Justinius' abridgement as producing a barren work. For authors: avoid excessive condensation that loses essential parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature's inventions are superior models
rubrics_metrics.description: Human ingenuity may devise various inventions ... yet will it never discover any inventions more beautiful, more simple or more practical than those of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural forms as models for design and evaluation (47). Guidance: favour solutions that mirror nature's simplicity and efficiency; consider natural function and economy when judging aesthetic or practical designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity is nature's governing principle; causation yields necessary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity is the mistress and guide of nature ... When anything is the cause of any other thing ... the movement of the effect necessarily follows the movement of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes deterministic causation (51–52). For reasoning and explanation, examine causes and expect consistent consequences unless impeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not renounce the senses for contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye, as lord of the senses, performs its duty in being an impediment to the confusion and lies of that which is not science but discourse ... his act of destroying his eyesight was madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises extreme withdrawal from senses (37). For learners and creators: preserve and trust sensory observation rather than artificially rejecting it; sensory evidence prevents false discursions.

rubrics_metrics.name: All knowledge originates from perception and the senses serve the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: All our knowledge is the offspring of our perceptions. The sense ministers to the soul, and not the soul sense ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims (35–36,70) that perception → common sense (brain) → memory; prioritize sensory-based evidence and clear images when forming knowledge or artistic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned manual actions become automatic through practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An example ... fingers, which learn to perform on an instrument the things which the intellect commands, and the lesson once learnt they will perform it without the aid of the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice internalizes complex actions (71). For artists and writers: cultivate repeated practice so techniques become automatic, freeing intellect for higher creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words that displease the ear will weary listeners; adapt length and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Words which do not satisfy the ear of the listener will always weary or annoy him ... when you observe such signs of vexation, shorten your speech or vary your argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical speaking/writing advice (109): attend to audience cues (yawns, frowns) and modify delivery accordingly. Anti-pattern: persisting in a tiresome argument and thereby incurring hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience mitigates insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Patience serves against insults as clothes do against the cold ... let thy patience increase under great offences, and they will not be able to hurt your feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral counsel (108): cultivate patience as a protective quality. Relevance for authors/speakers: patience in face of criticism preserves composure and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice is often rejected by those who most need it
rubrics_metrics.description: Here is a thing which the more it is needed the more it is rejected: and this is advice, which is unwillingly heeded by those who most need it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that recommendations may not be accepted by their intended recipients (110). For critics and teachers: expect resistance and tailor counsel accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate works relative to standards carefully; mismatches reveal development stages
rubrics_metrics.description: When the work comes up to the standard of the judgement, this is a bad sign for the judgement; and when the work excels the standard of the judgement, this is the worst sign ... and if the man is young ... he will grow into an excellent workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex evaluative principle (110): if a work merely meets the critic's standard it may indicate the standard is low; if it far exceeds it, danger of hubris; young creators who modestly exceed standards may develop into masters. Use standards diagnostically rather than absolutist scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward physiognomy and chiromancy; limited cues in faces/hands
rubrics_metrics.description: I will not dwell on false physiognomy and chiromancy because there is no truth in them ... it is true that the lineaments of the face partly reveal the character of men ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject pseudoscience yet acknowledge limited correlations (81): some facial features may hint temperament but such readings lack scientific foundation. Anti-pattern: overinterpreting physiognomy as deterministic in character studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural action is accomplished briefly
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural action is accomplished in the briefest manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For efficiency in action and design (58): favour brevity and economy in natural processes and, by analogy, in artistic expression or plot actions—avoid unnecessary prolongation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and respect variety in nature; avoid one-size rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature delight and abound in variety that among her trees there is not one plant to be found which is exactly like another ... not only among the plants, but among the boughs, the leaves and the fruits ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates (59–61) against rigid universal rules where natural variation is inherent; for artists, embrace individuality and avoid enforcing uniform templates where diversity is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study parts thoroughly to know the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The fervency of the love increases in proportion to the certainty of the knowledge, and the certainty issues from a complete knowledge of all the parts, which united compose the totality of the thing which ought to be loved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 48: detailed study of constituent parts leads to complete understanding. For writers/analysts: emphasize careful, comprehensive inquiry into components (characters, structure, details) before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and lasting merit over ephemeral riches or fame
rubrics_metrics.description: That which can be lost cannot be deemed riches. Virtue is our true wealth and the true reward of its possessor; it cannot be lost ... Nothing should be so greatly feared as empty fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical evaluative principle (92,111): value enduring moral qualities and substantive achievements over transient fame or external wealth when judging works or lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and use time purposefully; divide days to avoid living vainly
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us not lack ways and means of dividing and measuring these our wretched days, which we ought to take pleasure in spending and living not vainly ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel (95,76,93): structure time intentionally to produce lasting works and memory; for creators, plan and subdivide labor to avoid wasted effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: A well-spent life/work yields peaceful end
rubrics_metrics.description: As a well spent day affords happy sleep, so does a life profitably employed afford a happy death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral guideline (100): evaluate the meaningfulness of a life or oeuvre by usefulness and productive labour rather than mere length or notoriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: When empirical predictions fail, consider impediments rather than blaming experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Because given a principle, that which ensues from it is necessarily the true consequence of that principle, unless it be impeded. Should there ... be any obstacle, the effect ... will participate in the impediment ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological note (33): distinguish theoretical expectation from observed failure by diagnosing intervening obstacles; useful when experiments or creative intentions do not produce expected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose deceit and false trades; do not allow deception to go unmasked
rubrics_metrics.description: And many make a trade deceiving the foolish multitude, and if no one comes to unmask their deceits, they punish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical-professional injunction (105): critics, teachers and communities should call out frauds and expose false claims to protect the public and the integrity of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: The brain/common sense is central to perception and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'common sense' ... is situated in the centre of the head ... the senses transfer images to the perception, and the perception transfers them to the 'common sense' (brain), and by it they are stamped upon the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive model (70): when analyzing perception, cognition, or character psychology, use the chain: external object → sense → perception → common sense (brain) → memory; relevant for realistic depiction of mental processes.
